sentences.text: Globidens was an extinct genus of predatory marine lizard belonging to the family Mosasauridae, reaching a length of approximately 5 to 6 meters.
It is famous for its highly rounded, globe-like teeth, nearly 40 in number and similar in size to golf balls, which were embedded in the jaw so that only the tops were visible.
These semispherical teeth with rounded points were specifically adapted for crushing tough, armored prey like turtles, ammonites, nautili, and bivalves.
Stomach contents from a specimen found in South Dakota contained crushed shells of inoceramid clams.
The long, peg-shaped front teeth likely allowed Globidens to extract mollusks from the sea floor or pull them from rocks.
The genus Globidens was first described in 1912 by Charles W. Gilmore, who named the genus based on an incomplete specimen consisting of a partial skull, teeth, a cervical vertebra, and fragments.
The precise original location of the type specimen used by Gilmore is not precisely known, but the type species of the genus Globidens is Globidens alabamensis.
Recovery of a complete mandible and partial skull revealed large jaw muscle attachment points indicative of a diet of hard-shelled prey, and there are 32 recorded fossil occurrences of Globidens.

Globidens had a robust skull and a strong bite capable of penetrating the armor of shelled prey, and it is believed to have been a durophagous predator that ate hard-shelled mollusks like bivalves and ammonites.
This dentition was ideal for crushing the thick shells of mollusks like clams or hard-bodied crabs.
Globidens is classified within the subfamily Mosasaurinae and the tribe Globidensini, and it belongs to the family Mosasauridae.
Carinodens is regarded as a sister taxon to Globidens, but the specific phylogenetic placement of Globidens is somewhat unclear and varies between different studies.
Globidens lived during the Late Cretaceous in what is now North America, Morocco, Angola, and Indonesia, from the Coniacian to the Maastrichtian, between 89.8 and 66 million years ago.
Fossils of Globidens have been found in Angola, Brazil, Colombia, Morocco, Syria, and the United States.
